Two weeks, one real feature, and no need for another round of interviews.

That is how a founder described an engineering hire in a recent podcast clip. The candidate got a specific feature to build, asked questions, found their way around the codebase, and shipped it. After that, there was no longer any doubt about whether this person could do the job.

We think the same logic applies when a company chooses an engineering or AI partner.

Long evaluations tend to measure presentation: decks, case studies, references, rate cards. They rarely show how a team actually works on your code, with your constraints and your people.

A small, paid, fixed-scope trial tells you more:

How fast does the team understand an unfamiliar system?
What questions do they ask in the first days?
How visible is the work while it happens: commits, reviews, progress updates?
What is actually delivered at the end, and could your own team maintain it?

It costs a few weeks. It can save months with the wrong partner.

For AI work, the equivalent is a short pilot on your own data, with one clear success measure agreed upfront.

How do you test a partner today before signing a long contract?

The job hunt has changed. Are we changing with it?

Job searching in 2026 can feel strangely contradictory.

Unemployment may look stable, yet many candidates are spending months searching. Employers are not hiring at pace, but many still say they cannot find the right skills. Meanwhile, AI has made it easier than ever to apply and much harder to stand out.

Here is what I am seeing:
•	Applications per role have surged; LinkedIn reports candidates are submitting about 30% more applications than before the pandemic.

•	The average time to fill a role has risen from 41.4 days in 2022 to 61.5 days in the first eight months of 2026.

•	More than 27% of job seekers have been searching for 27 weeks or longer.

•	Employers increasingly use AI screening, while candidates use AI to tailor applications creating an “AI versus AI” bottleneck.

•	Skills-based hiring is growing, with many employers prioritising demonstrated capability over traditional qualifications.

So the question is no longer simply: “How many jobs can I apply to?”

It is: “How do I become memorable, credible, and discoverable in a crowded market?”

Some new rules I believe are worth discussing:

1.	Stop spraying, start positioning. A smaller number of well researched, well targeted applications will usually beat a high volume approach.

2.	Use AI as a thinking partner, not a replacement. Let it help you structure ideas but bring your own evidence, outcomes, voice, and judgement.

3.	Make your skills visible. Portfolios, case studies, projects, certifications, talks, writing, and measurable results matter more than a polished but generic CV.

4.	Prioritise humans, not just portals. Referrals, genuine networking, alumni connections, and conversations with people inside target companies can cut through automated screening.

5.	Treat the search like a campaign. Track outreach, follow up thoughtfully, build relationships, and review what is working every week.

6.	Stay open to non linear routes. Contract work, project-based roles, internal moves, and adjacent industries can create momentum when permanent roles are scarce.

The market is difficult but it is not closed. Healthcare, skilled trades, and other demand driven sectors continue to hire, while employers remain selective about capability and fit.

Over to you: What has changed most in your own job search over the past year? And what is one tactic that has actually helped you get noticed?

This month, one US state allowed an AI system to write a first prescription without a doctor deciding each case in advance.

The scope is narrow. Topical treatments for skin conditions, adults only. For the first 100 patients, two licensed doctors approve every prescription before it goes out. Only after that does the system get more room.

I think this is how it should be done. Small scope. Visible checks. Trust extended in stages, not declared on day one.

But one detail deserves more attention than the technology. In a related program in the same state, AI already renews prescriptions for chronic conditions, and the name of a licensed physician appears on each renewal.

A name on a decision that person did not make in the moment.

Medicine is simply the first place where this becomes visible. The same shift is happening quietly in credit decisions, hiring shortlists, contract reviews and investment memos. AI drafts. A human signs. Often in seconds.

Over the years I have signed term sheets, partnership agreements and, once, a lawsuit against someone I had trusted. What I learned is simple. A signature is the smallest unit of trust in any system. It says three things: I read this. I understood it. I could have refused.

When any of the three disappears, the signature becomes decoration. And decoration does not hold when something breaks.

The answer is not to stop machines from drafting. They will draft better than most of us. The answer is to protect the meaning of the signature:

- the signer sees what the machine saw, not only its conclusion
- refusing is fast, cheap and never punished
- the person whose name is on it can change the rules, not only approve them

Then a signature is still a promise. And promises are what trust is built from.

Trust = promises kept minus five times promises broken. A signature you never really gave still counts as a promise. It just counts against you.

Never sign what you did not decide.

Which decision in your work carries your name, but is no longer really yours?

At what stage does your people function/HR  get pulled into AI adoption?

It might seem pretty obvious, at the absolute inception of the strategic planning phase

But different organizations have different ways of working and there's somewhat a spectrum of how different companies approach this. It helps to look at the three distinct phases of maturity:

Stage 1: The Firefighter (Late Stage - Too Common): The executive team and IT select an AI vendor, sign the contract, and build the infrastructure. Right before rollout, they bring in HR to "manage the communication" or deal with employee anxiety and potential union pushback.

Stage 2: The Training Coordinator (Mid Stage - Transitioning): HR is brought in during the procurement phase to map out upskilling programs. They know the tech is coming, so they build training modules to ensure people know how to use the software. 

Stage 3: The Business Architect (Inception Stage - Ideal): HR sits at the table from day one alongside the CEO, CFO, and CIO. Before a single dollar is spent, HR helps define why the company is adopting AI, how it will redesign existing job roles, what future skills will be required, and how to build psychological safety so employees embrace the change instead of sabotaging it.

HR’s job is to translate technical capability into human capability, ensuring that AI is viewed by employees as a tool for augmentation and empowerment rather than an existential threat.

So, is your company currently leaning toward reactive deployment (IT-driven), proactive planning or are they trying to shift into a more strategic, early-stage role? or do you even think we should include AI conversations with regard to hiring let alone upskilling?

Your SAP system holds your most sensitive data. Now you’re adding AI on top of it. by Ruhani Garg Sharma
Employee records. Customer master data. Financial transactions. Pricing. Supplier contracts.
When Joule, embedded Business AI and custom models on SAP BTP start touching that data, three questions matter more than any demo:
1️⃣ Is it responsible? Is it fair, explainable and under human control?
2️⃣ Is it governed? Who owns it, who approved it, and who is monitoring it?
3️⃣ Is it private? Is personal data minimised, masked, retained only as long as needed, and kept out of prompts and logs?
I put together a practical guide that brings all three together. A few takeaways:
✅ Tier every AI use case by risk before you build or switch it on. A forecasting model and a candidate-ranking model should not go through the same gate.
✅ Make privacy by design a gate, not a checkbox. Run a DPIA for high-risk use cases and mask personal data before it reaches any model.
✅ Use what SAP already gives you. Authorisations, Read Access Logging, UI masking and ILM-based retention and blocking are your foundation.
✅ Don’t let AI bypass authorisations. Assistants running on privileged technical users can show people data they should never see. Carry the user’s identity through retrieval.
✅ Remember the hidden copies. AI logs, caches, embeddings and vector stores also hold personal data, and need retention and deletion rules too.
✅ Never copy unmasked production data into test. It’s still one of the most common sources of privacy incidents.
✅ Keep humans accountable. Decisions about hiring, pay or discipline should never be left to AI alone.
The guide also covers a governance operating model, RACI, KPIs, an AI incident playbook, a 12-month roadmap and ready-to-use checklists.

87,000 AI certificates. What should we measure next?

Nigeria’s ITF–NECA AI training initiative reportedly certified more than 87,000 participants in six months, from 101,000 registrations.

That is a significant training milestone.

But as a Workforce Economist, I have a question:

What happens after the certificate?

If we want to understand whether skills programmes are improving people’s economic prospects, we need to look beyond the number of people trained.

I would start with five questions:

1. Can participants actually do the work?
A certificate is evidence of completion. Can the participant demonstrate the skills in a real work setting?

2. Is there demand for those skills?
Are employers hiring?

 Are businesses looking for those capabilities? 

Are there realistic opportunities in the locations where participants live?

3. Are participants accessing opportunities?
Are they securing jobs, obtaining paid contracts, advancing in existing roles or building viable businesses?

4. Are their economic circumstances improving?
Are earnings increasing?

 Is work becoming more stable?

 Are participants moving into more productive opportunities?

5. Do the gains last?

Are participants still working and earning months later, or do the initial gains fade?

These questions matter because training completion, employment and economic progress are different outcomes.

And even when employment improves after training, we still need evidence to establish how much of that improvement the programme caused.

This is not an argument against AI training. It is an argument for measuring its value more completely.

Nigeria needs digital skills. But we also need to understand whether those skills translate into productive work and better livelihoods.

The real test of a skills programme is not just how many people receive certificates. It is what changes in their working lives afterwards.

If you were evaluating an AI skills programme, which outcome would you measure first: employment, earnings or sustained use of skills at work?

Interviewer asked me "How can we conduct contract testing using Playwright?" 

First correction I had to do: We cannot conduct contract testing as it natively cannot hold "consumer" & "provider" contracts. But we can explore "json-schema" validations. Which is the next best!

To understand json-schema validation we need 4 steps: 

1) Access to API spec (API Contract)
2) Create Json Schema (generate json schema using: )
3) Store json schema in your framework 
4) Use AJV/ZOD to compile schema and validate with response/request body used/received after execution of API test.

Always remember: JSON Schema validation is one technique used inside contract testing. It is not a synonym for contract testing itself.

What it covers: field presence, data types, required versus optional fields, string formats, nested structure. All of this is expressed once, declaratively, in a schema file.

What it cannot do: 
1) It cannot verify the HTTP status code or response headers were correct.
 
2) It cannot check semantic or business rules a type system cannot express, for example that end_date comes after start_date, or that a total matches the sum of line items.
 
3) It cannot tell you whether the schema reflects a real, agreed contract, or just whatever the API happened to return the one time it was sampled.

Quick tip: If you review the API spec carefully after every change made by Backend teams. Then we can use: "toJsonSchema" to dynamically generate schema using a flag. 

If set to true, it updates the schema files and we just validate the final playwright report.
